lead: Attenuation is the loss of optical power as light travels down a fiber. It is quoted as a coefficient in dB per kilometre, because a receiver needs a minimum power and every kilometre takes some away. The coefficient decides how far a link can reach before an amplifier or repeater is needed. A 1550 nm long-haul system, a 1310 nm campus link and a short 850 nm data link all use the same arithmetic.
prereq: You need: Unit 1 for the ray picture, total internal reflection and the meaning of guided power.

blocks.text: Let P<sub>in</sub> be the optical power launched into a fiber of length L km, and P<sub>out</sub> the power that leaves the far end. Both powers use the same unit, for example mW or µW. The attenuation coefficient is the loss per kilometre:

blocks.where: α is the attenuation coefficient in dB/km; L is the fiber length in km; P<sub>in</sub> is the input power; P<sub>out</sub> is the output power in the same unit; log₁₀ is the base-10 logarithm.

blocks.text: The loss over the whole length is A = α L dB, with A the total loss in dB. To go the other way, P<sub>out</sub> = P<sub>in</sub> × 10<sup>−A/10</sup>. Read 10<sup>−A/10</sup> as ten raised to the power (−A/10), not as 10 minus A/10.

Two anchor points make the decibel useful. A loss of 3 dB halves the power: 10 log₁₀(2) = 3.01 dB, so 3 dB means P<sub>out</sub>/P<sub>in</sub> is about 0.5. A loss of 10 dB divides power by ten. A gain of 3 dB doubles power. A 3 dB coupler is called that because each output is 3 dB (about half the power) below the input, which is an equal split between two ports.

sections.h3: Four loss families add in dB

blocks.text: Four families cover almost every loss in a fiber link. Each family gives its own dB value, and the total loss is the sum.

items: Absorption: intrinsic silica absorption and impurity absorption (see 2.2).
Bending: radiation loss when the fiber is curved (see 2.4).
Joint and connector loss: loss where two fibers meet (see Unit 3, Fiber joints, connectors and misalignment losses).

blocks.where: A<sub>total</sub> is the total loss in dB; each term on the right is that family's loss in dB.

blocks.text: The same addition works for coefficients in dB/km: α<sub>total</sub> = α<sub>abs</sub> + α<sub>scat</sub> + α<sub>bend</sub> + α<sub>joint</sub>. This works because dB is logarithmic: multiplying powers becomes adding dB. Do not add powers in mW and then convert; add the dB losses first, then convert once. A full link power budget, which combines these dB values with receiver sensitivity, is Unit 5.

sections.h3: Standard windows and the water peak

blocks.text: Silica fiber is not equally clear at all wavelengths. Three transmission windows matter in practice. The table also lists the water peak, which is a loss feature, not a usable window.

blocks.text: The water peak near 1380 nm comes from residual OH⁻ in older fiber; modern low-water-peak fiber reduces this bump. Long-haul links live at 1550 nm because each kilometre costs the fewest dB, so the distance between amplifiers is longest; erbium-doped fiber amplifiers also work in this band (see Unit 6).

Some syllabi give α in nepers per metre. Using the power definition P<sub>out</sub> = P<sub>in</sub> e<sup>−α<sub>Np</sub>L</sup>, 1 dB = 0.2303 nepers, and 1 Np = 4.343 dB. To convert a dB/km value to Np/km, multiply by 0.2303; to Np/m, divide by 1000 after that.

examples.question: A 1550 nm link uses fiber with α = 0.2 dB/km and launches 1 mW. (a) Find the loss over 80 km. (b) Find the power arriving at the far end. (c) Find the maximum length before the power falls to 1 µW.
steps: The loss over length L is A = α L. Here α = 0.2 dB/km and L = 80 km, so A = 0.2 × 80 = 16 dB.
The output power is P<sub>out</sub> = P<sub>in</sub> × 10^(−A/10). With P<sub>in</sub> = 1 mW, P<sub>out</sub> = 1 mW × 10^(−16/10) = 1 mW × 10^(−1.6).
10^(−1.6) = 0.025118..., so P<sub>out</sub> = 0.0251 mW, which is about 25 µW.
For the last part, the allowed loss is the dB ratio between 1 mW and 1 µW. Convert 1 µW to 0.001 mW, so allowed loss = 10 log₁₀(1 mW / 0.001 mW) = 10 log₁₀(1000) = 30 dB.
With the same fiber, L<sub>max</sub> = 30 dB / 0.2 dB/km = 150 km.
examples.answer: The loss over 80 km is 16 dB; the received power is about 0.0251 mW ≈ 25 µW; the maximum length before the power falls to 1 µW is 150 km.
examples.check:
import math
alpha = 0.2
L = 80.0
P_in_mW = 1.0
A = alpha * L
P_out_mW = P_in_mW * 10 ** (-A / 10)
allowed_dB = 10 * math.log10(P_in_mW / 0.001)
L_max = allowed_dB / alpha
print(f"{A:.1f}")
print(f"{P_out_mW:.4f}")
print(f"{L_max:.1f}")

traps: Writing A = α / L instead of A = α L. α is per kilometre, so multiplying by L kilometres cancels the km and leaves dB.
Mixing dB and dB/km in the same sum. Convert each loss to dB first; α values in dB/km must be multiplied by their lengths before adding.
Adding powers in mW and then taking a logarithm. Powers multiply through the fiber, so losses add in dB; convert only at the end.

Forgetting that a loss is positive. Since P<sub>out</sub> is less than P<sub>in</sub>, log₁₀(P<sub>in</sub>/P<sub>out</sub>) is positive; the formula with P<sub>out</sub>/P<sub>in</sub> gives a negative dB and must be read as loss.
Using 3 dB as exactly half. It is 3.01 dB; in a chain of many components the 0.01 dB can add up.

quiz.q: Define the attenuation coefficient of an optical fiber and give its usual unit.
quiz.a: It is the loss per unit length, α = (10/L) log₁₀(P<sub>in</sub>/P<sub>out</sub>), with L in km and the result in dB/km.

quiz.q: Why do we add losses in dB instead of adding powers in mW?
quiz.a: Optical powers multiply along the fiber: P<sub>out</sub> = P<sub>in</sub> × 10<sup>−A/10</sup>, that is, ten raised to the power (−A/10). Taking logarithms turns multiplication into addition, so dB losses add directly.

quiz.q: A fiber has α = 0.4 dB/km. Find the loss over 25 km and the output power if the input is 2 mW.
A link may lose 24 dB. If the fiber has α = 0.3 dB/km, what is the maximum fiber length, ignoring joints?
A 1310 nm link uses 60 km of fiber with α = 0.35 dB/km and four connectors each contributing 0.5 dB. Find the total loss.
quiz.a: Fiber loss = 0.35 × 60 = 21 dB. Connector loss = 4 × 0.5 = 2 dB. Total = 21 + 2 = 23 dB.

quiz.q: Why does 1550 nm give a longer unrepeated span than 850 nm for the same allowed loss? Use the standard numbers.
quiz.a: At 1550 nm α ≈ 0.2 dB/km; at 850 nm α ≈ 2.5 dB/km. For the same allowed loss, length scales as 1/α, so 1550 nm gives about 2.5/0.2 = 12.5 times the length, ignoring dispersion and other limits.

quiz.q: Convert α = 0.2 dB/km to nepers per metre, using the power definition.
quiz.a: 0.2 dB/km × 0.2303 Np/dB = 0.04606 Np/km. Divide by 1000 to get 4.606 × 10<sup>−5</sup> Np/m.

beyond: Not for the exam. In real networks the quoted 0.2 dB/km is a laboratory best; installed cable adds splice and bend loss, and aging and hydrogen can raise it. Modern coherent systems at 1550 nm use amplifiers every 80-120 km, and the loss limit is often traded against dispersion and nonlinearity. Low-water-peak fiber opened the 1380 nm band for coarse WDM.
